turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Well, I'm here because... well, honestly, it's been going on for months now. I keep seeing this same pattern over and over. My sister's appointments get moved around without anyone telling me, the bills show up wrong... and people just conveniently "forget" to call me back. Which reminds me, the mail carrier has been coming at such odd times lately. Usually, he's here right at 11:15, but yesterday it was almost 3:00. I was trying to organize my desk—I've been a supervisor for years, you know, so I like things orderly, everything in its place. I have this beautiful cherry wood organizer I bought at a craft fair in Vermont... oh, but anyway. Even when everyone tells me these things are just "mistakes" or "oversights," I know better. I know they're keeping information from me and trying to push me out of making decisions. Just like they did with the new filing system at work, but that's a whole other story.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, paranoid belief that others are intentionally keeping information from them and pushing them out of decisions, dismissing alternative explanations that these are just mistakes.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality and derailment, wandering off-topic to discuss the mail carrier's schedule, desk organization, and a cherry wood organizer before returning to the main point.

turns.doctor_question: When people tell you these things are just mistakes or oversights, do you think there's any possibility they might actually be right, or are you completely certain that they're deliberately keeping information from you?
turns.patient_response:
No, there’s no possibility it’s just a mistake. Like I was just saying, I know for an absolute fact that they are deliberately keeping information from me to push me out of the decision-making. You don’t supervise an office for as long as I have without learning how to spot when people are coordinating behind your back. 

I’ve trained dozens of administrative assistants, you know. Good help is so incredibly hard to find these days. The last girl we hired, Brenda, spent half her shift just looking down at her phone. I had to pull her into the conference room and explain that company time is company time. I actually had a special training manual printed up just for the new hires, with this lovely navy blue binding. I got the idea from a leadership seminar I attended in Chicago back in... oh, it must have been 2014. Or 2015? No, 2014, because it was freezing! The wind off the lake just cuts right through your layers. I actually had to run into Macy's and buy a whole new wool coat just to walk to the convention center. It had these beautiful tortoiseshell buttons... 

But, yes, anyway. I am completely certain. It's not an oversight, they just want me out of the loop.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses absolute certainty that people are deliberately keeping information from her and completely rejects the possibility of it being a mistake, demonstrating a fixed delusional belief.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, wandering far off-topic to discuss former employees, a training manual, a trip to Chicago, the weather, and a coat before eventually returning to the question.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever seen, heard, or experienced anything that other people around you couldn't perceive or didn't seem to notice—like voices, visions, or sensations that felt very real to you?
turns.patient_response: No, I've never had anything like that happen. I don't hear voices or see things that aren't there. I have very good hearing, actually. Better than most people my age. I always catch when my husband mumbles under his breath. He thinks I don't hear him, but I do. We've been married for thirty-two years, so you learn to pick up on those little sounds. We met at a friend's barbecue, actually. He made the most incredible potato salad. It had dill in it, which I never thought to add, but it really brightens up the flavor. I asked him for the recipe, but he said it was a family secret. His grandmother brought it over from Germany. She was a seamstress, made the most beautiful dresses. But no, to answer your question, my senses are perfectly fine. I don't see or hear anything unusual. It's just what people are actually doing that's the problem.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, wandering off-topic from the question about hallucinations to discuss potato salad recipes and her husband's grandmother's profession.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing voices or seeing things that are not there.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back over your life, have you always been somewhat suspicious of people's motives and worried that others might be trying to take advantage of you, or did these concerns about people deliberately keeping information from you start more recently—like within the past few weeks or months?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, no, definitely not my whole life. I've always been a very reasonable, trusting person—maybe too trusting sometimes, honestly. No, this specific situation... it’s been going on for about 11 months now. It all really started when my sister’s health suddenly got worse, and I had to step in and start coordinating her care. 

She goes to that new medical center off Route 4. Have you seen that building? It’s almost entirely glass on the outside. It looks very modern, but I always think it must cost an absolute fortune to heat in the winter. And the parking lot is just a nightmare. They designed it with these incredibly tight angles, so if anyone has a larger vehicle, they end up taking up two spaces. My husband drives a Honda CR-V, which isn't even that big, but the last time I borrowed it to go pick up her prescriptions—oh, the pharmacy line was practically out the door that day. They only had one technician working, this young boy who clearly didn't know how to use the register system. He kept hitting the wrong override key. I almost offered to step behind the counter and show him how to process a basic transaction, because it’s just basic data entry, really. 

But... well, where was I? Yes, about 11 months ago, when I had to take over her schedule. That's when I noticed people were deliberately messing with the appointments and keeping things from me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a persecutory belief that people are deliberately messing with appointments and keeping information from them.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, wandering off-topic into a long tangent about a medical building, parking, and a pharmacy technician before losing their train of thought.

turns.doctor_question: When you think about the possibility that your sister's appointments might be changed by mistake, or that the bills could have errors, or that people simply forgot to call you back—do you ever find yourself thinking 'well, maybe that could have happened,' even for just a moment, or does it always feel absolutely certain to you that it's deliberate?
turns.patient_response:
No, I don't think "maybe" for a second. I know it's deliberate. I've been seeing this exact same pattern for months now—her appointments get moved without my permission, the bills show up with all these "errors," and the nurses conveniently "forget" to call me back. They say it's just mistakes, but I know for a fact they are keeping information from me and trying to push me out of her care decisions. 

It's just like when you try to call the cable company. Have you tried calling them recently? You sit on hold for forty-five minutes listening to that awful elevator music. It’s always that same smooth jazz track with the saxophone that sounds slightly out of tune. My husband plays the saxophone, actually. He played in a jazz band in college. They were called the Midnight Cats, or something silly like that. They played at our wedding reception. We had the reception at this lovely little country club that had these gorgeous weeping willow trees out by the golf course. The catering was spectacular, though they did run out of the stuffed mushrooms before my aunt could get any. She complained about it for years. She was a very particular woman, my aunt. She used to iron her bedsheets. Can you imagine having the time to iron bedsheets? 

But yes, to answer your question, it's absolutely certain. They are doing it on purpose to push me out, no matter what they claim.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses absolute, unwavering certainty that others are deliberately conspiring to push her out of her sister's care, demonstrating a fixed false belief.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient displays tangential speech, drifting from the topic of her sister's care to the cable company, elevator music, her husband's saxophone, their wedding, and her aunt's ironing habits.

turns.doctor_question: Before this situation with your sister's care started 11 months ago, did you generally tend to question people's motives and worry that they might be trying to harm you or take advantage of you in other areas of your life—like at work, in friendships, or with family?
turns.patient_response: No, no, not at all. Like I said before, I've always been a very trusting person. Maybe a bit too trusting, if I'm being honest. I never used to worry about people having hidden agendas or trying to trick me. At work, I manage a team of administrative support staff, and I've always had a wonderful relationship with them. Well, most of them. There was this one temp we hired a few years ago, Sarah. She was supposed to be helping with filing, but I constantly found her just staring out the window at the parking lot. We overlook a bakery, you see. The smell of fresh bread around 10 AM is just intoxicating. They make this sourdough that has jalapeños and cheddar baked right into the crust. I tried making sourdough during the pandemic, like everyone else did, but my starter died after two weeks. I named him Dough-boy. My husband thought it was hilarious, but I was actually quite sad when it went bad. It smelled like old gym socks. You know that smell when someone leaves damp towels in a gym bag for a week? My son used to do that when he played soccer in high school. We had to throw out three different duffel bags because the smell just wouldn't wash out. But anyway, before all this started with my sister's care, I never had any reason to doubt people's motives. I just went about my life assuming everyone was doing their job properly.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality and derailment, wandering from a story about a coworker to a bakery, sourdough bread, the pandemic, gym socks, and their son's soccer bags before returning to the original topic.

turns.doctor_question: When you think back to your work relationships over the years before your sister's situation started, were there ever times when you felt annoyed or frustrated with coworkers because you wondered if they were being honest with you, or if maybe they were trying to make you look bad—even if you didn't dwell on it at the time?
turns.patient_response:
No, not really. I mean, sure, there were normal office frustrations, but I never thought anyone was deliberately trying to sabotage me or lie to me. Mostly I just got annoyed when people wouldn't refill the coffee pot. That drives me absolutely crazy. 

We had this Keurig machine in the breakroom for a while, but then management decided it was too expensive to keep buying the little pods, so they switched us back to a standard drip coffee maker. It was a Bunn, I think? One of those commercial ones that brews a whole pot in three minutes. But nobody ever wanted to change the filter. My coworker, Linda—she was one of the worst offenders. She retired last year, actually. We threw her a lovely party. We ordered a sheet cake from that bakery I mentioned earlier, the one across the street. It was half vanilla, half chocolate, with this thick buttercream frosting. The frosting was dyed this incredibly bright blue color because Linda's favorite color was turquoise. But it stained everyone's teeth! 

We had a big department meeting right after the party, and all of us were sitting around the conference table looking like we had been eating blue popsicles. The regional director was visiting that day, too. He was wearing this very expensive-looking grey suit with a tie that had tiny little sailboats on it. My father used to sail. He had a little Sunfish boat that we'd take out on the lake during the summer... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, about people making me look bad. No, no, nothing like that. Like I said, before all this nonsense with my sister's care started, I just assumed everyone was doing their best. I never had any reason to worry about my coworkers' motives.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from coffee machines to a retirement party, blue frosting, a director's tie, and her father's sailboat before losing her train of thought.

turns.doctor_question: Looking at your relationships more broadly—with your husband, your son, your friends—have you generally felt that people are trustworthy and have your best interests in mind, or have you often felt on guard that people might not be telling you the truth or might be working against you in some way?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, completely trustworthy. I've never felt on guard with my family or my friends. My husband and I have been married for thirty-two years, and I trust him with my life. We actually just celebrated our anniversary last month. We went to this little Italian place downtown—Mario's, I think it was? It had those classic red and white checkered tablecloths. 

We both ordered the chicken parmigiana, but honestly, the sauce was a bit too salty. I make a much better marinara at home. The secret is to add just a tiny pinch of sugar to cut the acidity of the tomatoes. I learned that from my mother. She used to grow her own tomatoes in the backyard when I was growing up. Big, beautiful heirloom tomatoes. She had this huge garden with zucchini, squash, and cucumbers. One year we had so many cucumbers we had to learn how to pickle them just so they wouldn't go to waste. We spent an entire weekend sterilizing mason jars in the kitchen. It was so hot and humid in that house, we had all the windows open and the box fans running, but it still felt like a sauna in there... 

Oh, but anyway. No, I don't worry about my husband or my son or my friends lying to me. I know they have my best interests at heart. I've never been a suspicious person with the people in my life. It's just the people at my sister's facility that I know for a fact are working against me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, persecutory belief that the people at her sister's facility are 'working against me.'
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential and circumstantial speech, drifting into a long, loosely associated story about marinara sauce and pickling cucumbers before returning to the question.

turns.doctor_question: If someone you completely trusted—like your husband—sat down with you and showed you documentation proving that your sister's appointments were changed due to a legitimate scheduling software error, would you be able to accept that explanation, or would you still believe they were deliberately changed?
turns.patient_response:
Well, if my husband showed me that... you know, he's always trying to show me things on his iPad anyway. Just last night he was showing me this video of a Golden Retriever trying to catch snowflakes. We used to have a Golden, actually. His name was Buster. He was such a good boy, but he chewed right through the baseboards in the hallway when he was a puppy. We had to hire a contractor to come fix it, and the man tracked mud all over my brand new hallway runner. It was a Persian rug, beautiful deep reds and navy blues. I got it at an estate sale over in Westlake. The woman who died had the most incredible collection of antique lamps, too. I almost bought one with a stained glass shade, but I didn't have anywhere to put it in our living room... 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, the scheduling software. 

No, even if my husband sat me down and showed me a printout or a computer screen saying it was a glitch, I wouldn't buy it. I’m here because for months now I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern. It's not just one software error. My sister’s appointments get moved, her bills show up wrong, people at the facility conveniently 'forget' to call me back. And even when everyone says it’s just mistakes or a computer issue, I know what's really going on. I know they’re keeping information from me and trying to push me out of decisions regarding her care. A piece of paper isn't going to change what I know they are doing.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient demonstrates a fixed belief that people are conspiring against her regarding her sister's care, explicitly stating she would not change her mind even if presented with proof of a software glitch.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality, drifting from the topic of her husband's iPad to a dog, a contractor, a rug, and antique lamps before losing her train of thought.
